body:
Why these Gujarat sites matter

Harappan settlements in Gujarat shared features with the wider civilisation, but they also developed regional building styles, pottery traditions and agricultural practices. Three sites illustrate different aspects of this history: Surkotada in Kutch, and Rangpur and Rojdi in Saurashtra.

They are particularly useful for distinguishing the Mature Harappan urban tradition from local developments that continued during and after the decline of major Harappan cities.

Surkotada: a fortified settlement in Kutch

Surkotada is situated in present-day Kutch district, Gujarat. Excavations revealed a compact Harappan settlement with a fortified citadel and an adjoining residential area. Its walls and buildings show that defensive or enclosing structures were not confined to the largest Harappan cities.

The reported horse remains

Surkotada is widely associated with reports of horse and ass remains. The excavator's published report described bones assigned to horse and ass from the settlement. The identification and wider significance of the reported horse remains have been debated, particularly in discussions of the presence of domestic horses in Harappan times.

The precise statement to remember is that horse remains were reported from Surkotada. This should not be expanded into a claim that domesticated horses were common throughout Harappan civilisation or that the disputed identification settles the question for all sites.

Rangpur: Harappan pottery and later ceramic continuity

Rangpur is an archaeological site in Saurashtra, Gujarat. Its occupation sequence is important because it shows changes in pottery from Harappan forms through modified regional traditions into later ceramic styles.

A particularly important association is Lustrous Red Ware. This is pottery with a noticeably shiny or burnished red surface. It began appearing in later levels at Rangpur and became prominent in a subsequent pottery tradition.

The term lustrous describes the surface finish. Lustrous Red Ware is not simply another name for all red pottery made during the Mature Harappan period.

Rangpur is useful for understanding continuity and change. Harappan occupation did not necessarily end with an immediate replacement by an unrelated population. Some local pottery traditions developed out of earlier Harappan forms.

Rojdi: the Sorath Harappan tradition

Rojdi is in present-day Rajkot district, Saurashtra, Gujarat, near the Bhadar River. It is especially associated with the Sorath Harappan regional tradition.

Excavations revealed remains of settlement structures, including stone or rubble foundations, as well as pottery, beads and other objects. Evidence of millet cultivation helps explain the importance of agriculture to communities in this part of Gujarat.

The term Sorath Harappan identifies a regional form of Harappan material culture associated particularly with Saurashtra. Such communities shared connections with the wider Harappan tradition while using distinctive local pottery and building practices.

Rojdi has an occupational sequence extending across the broad Mature-to-Late Harappan transition. It should therefore not be treated as a site belonging exclusively to a single short phase.

Three sites, three distinguishing features

Surkotada is most readily associated with a fortified settlement and reported horse remains. Rangpur is particularly associated with the development of later pottery, including Lustrous Red Ware. Rojdi is associated with the Sorath Harappan tradition, settlement remains and millet cultivation.

These sites also show why the Late Harappan period cannot be understood simply as the disappearance of people. Settlement patterns and cultural expressions changed, but communities remained active in different parts of Gujarat.

Prelims focus

  • Surkotada: Kutch, Gujarat; fortified Harappan settlement.
  • Surkotada is associated with reported horse and ass remains; the horse identification and its significance have been debated.
  • Rangpur: Saurashtra, Gujarat; later ceramic sequence and Lustrous Red Ware.
  • Rojdi: Rajkot district, Gujarat; Sorath Harappan tradition.
  • Rojdi has evidence of millet cultivation and stone-founded settlement structures.
  • Trap: Rangpur's Lustrous Red Ware should not be confused with the entire Mature Harappan pottery tradition.

[GCERT, History, Standard 11, Chapter 2, Harappan Civilisation, pp. 7–8; Archaeological Survey of India, J. P. Joshi, Excavation at Surkotada and Exploration in Kutch, 1990, pp. 14–18, 381, as reproduced by Gujarat Tourism, consulted 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, S. R. Rao, Excavation at Rangpur and Other Explorations, section on pottery and cultural sequence; Archaeological Survey of India, Indian Archaeology 1993–94: A Review, section 35, Excavation at Rojdi, District Rajkot; Kuldeep K. Bhan, Review of Prehistoric Cultures of Gujarat and Need to Develop Accurate Settlement Gazetteer, section Rojdi: The Emergence of the Sorath Harappan; Pokharia, Kharakwal and Srivastava, Archaeobotanical Evidence of Millets in the Indian Subcontinent, Journal of Archaeological Science, 2014, pp. 442–455.]

title: Gujarat's Regional Harappan Sites: Surkotada, Rangpur and Rojdi

body:
The eight-site reference atlas

When identifying a Harappan site, connect 3 pieces of information: its name, its present-day location and the particular discovery associated with it. A single site may have several discoveries, but some are especially useful for distinguishing it from similarly named or nearby settlements.

SitePresent-day locationKey evidence or association
ShortughaiAfghanistanTraces of canals; location near lapis lazuli sources
BanawaliHaryana, Fatehabad districtTerracotta model of a plough
SurkotadaGujarat, KutchFortified settlement; reported horse and ass remains
Ropar or RupnagarPunjab, IndiaHarappan cemetery; seal-related finds; first Harappan site excavated in independent India
RakhigarhiHaryana, Hisar districtExtensive Early and Mature Harappan settlement; burial grounds
KalibanganRajasthan, Hanumangarh districtEarly Harappan ploughed field with crossing furrows; structures interpreted as fire altars
RangpurGujarat, SaurashtraHarappan ceramic sequence and later Lustrous Red Ware
RojdiGujarat, Rajkot district, SaurashtraSorath Harappan pottery; settlement remains; millet cultivation

Identify the type of evidence before matching the site

Agricultural evidence

Banawali, Kalibangan and Shortughai are associated with different agricultural clues. The plough model belongs to Banawali, the ploughed field to Kalibangan and the canal traces to Shortughai. Rojdi adds evidence of millet cultivation in Saurashtra.

Settlement and burial evidence

Surkotada is especially associated with fortification. Ropar and Rakhigarhi have burial evidence, but their locations and broader significance differ. Ropar is in Punjab on the Sutlej, while Rakhigarhi is an exceptionally extensive site in Haryana with Early and Mature Harappan remains.

Pottery and regional culture

Rangpur is especially important for the development of Lustrous Red Ware in later ceramic levels. Rojdi is associated with the Sorath Harappan regional tradition. Both demonstrate the importance of Gujarat to the history of Harappan cultural change.

Combine the chronology with the atlas

Knowing the site name is not always enough. A discovery may belong to a particular stage of occupation rather than every period represented at that site.

At Kalibangan, the ploughed field is associated with the Early Harappan occupation, although the site also has Mature Harappan remains. Rakhigarhi preserves evidence from Early and Mature Harappan phases. Rojdi's regional settlement sequence extends across the broad Mature-to-Late transition. At Rangpur, the later pottery sequence shows how material culture changed after the classic urban period.

Therefore, the correct relationship may involve site, state, discovery and phase. These details should remain separate until a statement requires them to be combined.

Distinctions that prevent common mistakes

  • Banawali versus Kalibangan: A clay plough model was found at Banawali; preserved furrows of an actual ploughed field were found at Kalibangan.
  • Ropar versus Rakhigarhi: Ropar is in Punjab; Rakhigarhi is in Haryana. Both have Harappan burial evidence.
  • Shortughai versus the Indian sites: Shortughai is in Afghanistan, not in an Indian state.
  • Surkotada versus Rangpur: Surkotada is linked with fortification and reported horse remains; Rangpur is a key site for later pottery developments.
  • Rangpur versus Rojdi: Rangpur is closely associated with Lustrous Red Ware; Rojdi is associated with the Sorath Harappan regional tradition.
  • Mature versus Late Harappan: The decline of large, standardised urban centres did not bring all regional settlement activity to an immediate end.

Prelims focus

  • Banawali: terracotta plough model; Haryana.
  • Kalibangan: Early Harappan crossed plough furrows; Rajasthan.
  • Shortughai: canals; Afghanistan.
  • Ropar: Sutlej, Punjab; Harappan cemetery and seal-related finds.
  • Rakhigarhi: extensive Early and Mature Harappan settlement; Haryana.
  • Gujarat: Surkotada for fortification and reported horse remains, Rangpur for later Lustrous Red Ware, and Rojdi for Sorath Harappan culture.
  • Trap: A site associated with several phases should not automatically have every one of its discoveries assigned to the Mature Harappan period.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, pp. 1–4, 12, 15, 17; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 89–96; Government of Punjab, Rupnagar District Administration, Archaeological Museum, consulted 17 November 2026; Ministry of Culture, Government of India, Rakhigarhi press release, 22 June 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Excavations at Kalibangan: The Harappans, Chapter 1; Archaeological Survey of India, J. P. Joshi, Excavation at Surkotada and Exploration in Kutch, 1990; Archaeological Survey of India, S. R. Rao, Excavation at Rangpur and Other Explorations; Archaeological Survey of India, Indian Archaeology 1993–94: A Review, section 35, Excavation at Rojdi, District Rajkot.]
